title: The prodigal son didn’t just leave home—he rejected identity (Luke 15:12)
paragraphs: The prodigal son didn’t just leave home—he rejected identity (Luke 15:12)
He didn’t just ask for money.
He asked for distance.
“The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me…’” (Luke 15:12).

That wasn’t just a financial request.
It was a relational rupture.
In that culture, asking for the inheritance before the father died was like saying, “I want what’s yours, but I don’t want you.”

That’s the ache inside prodigal living.
Not just leaving home.
Rejecting identity.
He walked away from sonship before he ever walked into the far country.
And that’s how sin works.

It does not begin in the pigpen.
It begins in the heart.
It whispers, Take the gifts. Leave the Father. Define yourself. Spend your life your own way.
But here’s what we miss:

The prodigal did not lose his value in the far country.
He lost his clarity.

He was still a son.
But he was living like an orphan.
And some of us are doing the same.

Chasing freedom that becomes slavery.
Demanding control that becomes collapse.
Running from the Father while starving for the very love we rejected.
But grace walks faster than shame.

When the son came to himself, he returned with a speech.
The father answered with an embrace.
That is the Gospel.

We were the ones who ran.
We traded identity for independence.
We burned through mercy like it was ours to waste.
But in Christ, the Father does not merely tolerate repentant sinners—He runs to redeem them.

Jesus is the reason prodigals can come home.
Jesus is the robe for our shame, the ring for our belonging, the feast for our restoration.

So no—
the prodigal son didn’t just leave home.
He rejected identity.
But the Father, through Christ, restores what rebellion tried to erase.

Come home.
You were never made for the far country.
